title: Scientists Find Dinosaur Blood That Survived 115 Million Years
summary: Scientists have found traces of dinosaur blood inside bones that are 115 million years old. The discovery shows that biological molecules can survive far longer than researchers once believed. An international team led by Curtin University in Australia studied the limb bones of Aratasaurus museunacionali, a meat-eating dinosaur found in Brazil. Inside tiny passages that once held blood vessels, the team found fossilized red blood cells. Chemical tests revealed heme molecules, parts of hemoglobin, the protein that lets red blood cells carry oxygen. The team also found amino acids linked to collagen, a structural protein found in bones and other connective tissues. This is the first time scientists have found chemical proof of hemoglobin-derived molecules inside fossilized dinosaur red blood cells. So how did the blood survive? Part of the answer is a mineral called hausmannite, which helped stabilize the cells and protect their molecules. The dinosaur was probably buried quickly in sediment with little oxygen, conditions that may have slowed the usual breakdown of biological material. Professor Kliti Grice, who led the study, called the find a landmark discovery.
why_it_matters: It shows that tiny clues from long ago can still teach us how living things worked, just like clues in your own body help us learn how you stay healthy.

background_read: Dinosaurs lived on Earth long ago, and their bones can turn into fossils over a very long time.
Blood is made of tiny parts, like red blood cells that carry oxygen around the body, and those parts usually break down quickly after an animal dies.
Scientists study old bones to learn how living things worked, and this find shows that tiny pieces of blood can sometimes survive inside bones for a very long time.
